video_title: Zac Prince on BlockFi, Bitcoin, and GalaxyOne
gist: Zac Prince gives a first-hand post-mortem of BlockFi's collapse — a $100M regulatory penalty mid-fundraise, an 85% bank run that took client assets from ~$12B to ~$2B in two weeks, and an FTX acquisition undone by falsified Alameda balance sheets he saw as a cooperating trial witness — then lays out how a sharply reduced risk appetite shapes Galaxy One: no rehypothecation, no crypto lending, a $250M-capped 8% Galaxy-guaranteed cash product, a sub-9% crypto portfolio line of credit, and an explicit refusal to add prediction markets. He also argues the 60/40 portfolio and the 1%-of-AUM RIA model are ripe for unbundling, and flags Galaxy's second business — a 5+ gigawatt Texas AI data center pipeline — as the firm's other engine.

insights.claim: Zac Prince attributes BlockFi's failure to exactly three sequential shocks — the summer 2021 state securities actions, the May 2022 Celsius/Voyager-triggered bank run, and the FTX acquisition — rather than to a single underwriting mistake.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: A useful template for diagnosing levered financial platforms: regulatory capital shock first weakens the balance sheet, a liquidity run then removes the revenue base, and distress M&A becomes the only exit.
insights.quote: if we just think about what caused BlockFi to end in tragedy the way that it did, there were three big moments

insights.claim: The state-level enforcement wave against BlockFi's interest accounts began in New Jersey, and within one to two weeks roughly eight states had copy-pasted essentially the same order, showing regulatory contagion moves faster than company response cycles.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: For any fintech or crypto platform, a single state action should be underwritten as an eight-state action within a fortnight — size the legal and capital reserve accordingly.
insights.quote: It actually started in New Jersey and then within a week or two there were uh I think eight states that had essentially copy and pasted the order from New Jersey.

insights.claim: BlockFi's $100 million settlement was an order-of-magnitude outlier versus comparable fintech precedents such as PayPal's money-transmission fights and Lending Club's SEC dispute, where fines were immaterial relative to a billion-dollar-plus market leader's balance sheet.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: Evidence that crypto-sector enforcement was priced punitively rather than proportionally — relevant to how investors underwrite regulatory tail risk in any newly-regulated category.
insights.quote: in in just about every case outside of crypto that you look at, the fine was not significant relative to the size of the company's balance sheet

insights.claim: The $100 million fine landed mid-close of a $500 million funding round in which roughly half the money had already been wired, causing investors to get cold feet and forcing a dramatic downsizing with an opt-out for every participant.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: Shows how enforcement timing alone — not business performance — can vaporize committed primary capital; a signed term sheet is not funded capital until wired.
insights.quote: all the docs have been signed and all the money has been wired about half of $500 million had already been wired by investors

insights.claim: BlockFi peaked at a little over $14 billion in client assets in summer 2021, drifted to about $12 billion by May 2022, then fell from $12 billion to $2 billion in the first two weeks after Celsius and Voyager blew up — roughly an 85% withdrawal that BlockFi processed in full.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: Concrete calibration for modeling run severity at yield-bearing crypto platforms: assume the deposit base can shrink ~85% in two weeks once a peer fails.
insights.quote: 12 billion down to 2 billion

insights.claim: BlockFi had switched from growth mode to profitability mode and was profitable for the first time in its history in the months before May 2022, but the deposit run destroyed the revenue base and flipped it back to unprofitable while still solvent.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: Illustrates that solvency and viability diverge — a firm can process every withdrawal and still be forced into a 6-18 month capital-raise clock.
insights.quote: the company was actually profitable for the first time it in its history for a few months leading up to May of 2022

insights.claim: BlockFi's SEC settlement required not just paying $100 million but registering its interest account as a security — which would have been the first product of its kind issued fully legally as a registered security — and completing that registration was a core reason to seek FTX's capital.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: The registered-yield-product path existed and was nearly built; whoever revives it inherits a template regulators already blessed.
insights.quote: register our interest account as a security and it's going to be the first product of its kind that's issued fully legally as a as a security

insights.claim: For technical reasons BlockFi was never formally part of FTX — FTX held a one-year option to acquire it that it was planning to exercise — so BlockFi remained an independent company and Prince stayed CEO through confirmation of its bankruptcy plan.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: Corrects the common assumption that BlockFi was an FTX subsidiary; the structure is why its estate wound down and distributed to creditors separately.

themes.theme: Alameda's Falsified Balance Sheets and Counterparty Diligence Failure

insights.claim: As a cooperating witness for the prosecution, Prince learned that Alameda sent lenders including BlockFi balance sheets that were simply false, with Caroline Ellison producing seven or eight spreadsheet tabs of varying degrees of lies and Sam Bankman-Fried selecting the most misleading version over Slack.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: Document-based counterparty credit diligence is worthless against a counterparty manufacturing the documents — the failure mode that no standard lending framework catches.
insights.quote: she would create seven tabs on the spreadsheet, seven or eight tabs, all in kind of varying degrees of essentially lies. And then Sam would write back over Slack and he would pick the one that was like essentially the biggest lie.

insights.claim: By BlockFi's own credit and collateral framework — overseen by a board including finance professionals from some of the largest banks in the world — FTX screened as one of crypto's best-capitalized counterparties and one of the most willing to post collateral, sometimes in Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana but in some cases in FTT.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: Accepting a counterparty's own native token as collateral converts a secured loan into an unsecured bet on that counterparty — the single diligence line item to police.
insights.quote: they were consistently within the crypto market, one of the best capitalized counterparties from a balance sheet and financial statement perspective, and one of the most willing to post collateral counterparties

insights.claim: Prince's read on Sam Bankman-Fried before the acquisition was that FTX was becoming a genuine threat to Binance for the largest exchange in the world and was a money-printing machine — which is precisely why the idea that the money wasn't there never crossed his mind.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: Business-model quality was used as a proxy for solvency; investors should treat 'the unit economics are too good to fail' as a diligence blind spot, not comfort.
insights.quote: I had seen some chirping on Twitter, but it had never crossed my mind that the money wouldn't be there. You own a money printing machine.

insights.claim: Prince received and acted on explicit advice that the right move in a financial crisis is to attach your boat to a bigger boat that can weather the storm — a heuristic that failed because the bigger boat was itself fraudulent.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: Distress-M&A rescue logic is only as good as the acquirer's balance sheet integrity; in opaque sectors the 'strong hands' rescue can be the terminal risk.
insights.quote: attach your boat to a bigger boat, something that can weather the storm

themes.theme: The Crypto War Post-Mortem and Regulatory Pendulum

insights.claim: Prince argues crypto banks' collapse was financially over-determined, not crypto-specific: several of the largest traditional banks including Silicon Valley Bank failed in the same three-to-six month window, so anyone reading financial history would have predicted the less-regulated crypto banks would go down too.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: Reframes 2022-23 crypto failures as a rates-and-duration banking event with a crypto overlay, which matters for how much of the sector's risk premium should persist today.
insights.quote: traditional banks have collapsed. What do you think happens to the crypto banks?

insights.claim: Prince draws a hard line between firms that objectively committed fraud (FTX, Celsius) and firms that objectively did not (Silvergate, Silicon Valley Bank), arguing regulators and the public wrongly painted the entire category with a single brush.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: Suggests mispricing in how surviving crypto-adjacent financial institutions are still discounted for reputational rather than actual credit risk.
insights.quote: some fraud therefore all companies in this category bad and we need to shut the whole thing down

insights.claim: Prince points listeners to Alan Lane's Substack post published that morning as the fullest account yet of what led Silvergate to a voluntary wind-down despite processing every customer withdrawal and remaining solvent.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: A solvent, fully-liquid regulated bank choosing wind-down is the strongest available evidence for de-banking-by-supervision as a real risk factor.

insights.claim: Pompliano argues the anti-crypto regulatory campaign was far more successful than critics admit — it did not stop Bitcoin or the major coins, but it killed FTX and other companies and left even Binance wounded rather than dead.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Protocol-level assets proved regulation-resistant while intermediaries did not — an argument for owning the asset over the operating company through policy cycles.
insights.quote: I don't think we give them enough credit for how successful they were. Like they did not stop Bitcoin.

insights.claim: Prince contends the regulatory calculus ignored that a crypto world with regulated options from BlackRock and Fidelity plus publicly traded crypto companies producing audited quarterly financials is strictly better than the alternative, since the technology cannot be put back in the box.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: Frames the ETF-and-public-company era as the intended consumer-protection outcome, supporting continued institutional share gain over offshore venues.

insights.claim: Prince warns the pendulum may now have swung too far under the current administration, specifically citing permissiveness toward certain forms of gambling and meme coins as the mirror-image policy error.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: A pro-crypto operator flagging over-permissiveness is an early signal that speculative-product regulation is the next policy risk to underwrite.
insights.quote: maybe the pendulum has swung a little too far with this administration in terms of allowing certain things uh to happen, whether that's certain forms of gambling or or things with meme coins

insights.claim: Pompliano's mimetic-politics framework holds that partisan counter-positioning — Democrats anti-crypto, Trump pro-crypto, then opponents becoming anti-Trump-crypto — is painful for operators but is paradoxically the mechanism that eventually produces clear rules demanded by a silent majority.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Implies regulatory clarity arrives through political volatility rather than despite it — a reason to expect codified rules on a multi-cycle rather than linear timeline.

themes.theme: Galaxy One's Deliberately De-Risked Product Design

insights.claim: Galaxy One operates with no rehypothecation on the platform and no crypto lending at all, a deliberate structural break from the BlockFi model rather than a tightened version of it.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: The two design choices that caused 2022's contagion are removed by construction — the key diligence question to ask of any successor yield platform.
insights.quote: no rehypothecation on our platform uh and no crypto lending

insights.claim: Prince now believes crypto lending is really hard and maybe even impossible to scale because Bitcoin does not natively produce a yield, so manufacturing one forces the operator progressively out the risk spectrum as assets grow.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: A structural, not cyclical, indictment of the crypto-yield business model — treat scale in any BTC yield product as a risk signal rather than a success metric.
insights.quote: crypto lending is is really hard to scale maybe even impossible uh to scale bitcoin doesn't produce a yield trying to get it to is is very challenging and as you scale you're kind of forced to go out on the risk spectrum

insights.claim: Galaxy Premium Yield pays accredited investors 8% on cash, is hard-capped at $250 million against a Galaxy institutional lending book with principal outstanding well north of $1 billion, and carries a guarantee from Galaxy, a NASDAQ-listed company with a market cap north of $10 billion.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: The cap-to-book ratio and parent guarantee are the actual credit structure to underwrite — 8% cash yield is a claim on Galaxy's balance sheet, not on a segregated pool.
insights.quote: We capped the size of our premium yield product on the Galaxy 1 app at $250 million, which is just a fraction of its overall institutional lending book, and then Galaxy put a guarantee on it.

insights.claim: Galaxy Premium Yield's liquidity terms were shortened from a 60-day to a 30-day duration, with a variable rate changeable on 30 days' notice that has not moved since launch roughly a year ago.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: Gating terms are the real risk disclosure in any cash-yield product; shortening duration while holding rate signals confidence in the underlying lending book.

insights.claim: Prince's source of the 8% is that crypto capital markets remain more expensive than traditional capital markets on a risk-adjusted basis, so Galaxy earns the spread through institutional lending it already does rather than by taking incremental risk for the retail product.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: The persistence of that cross-market spread is the single variable that determines whether 8% retail cash yields survive; watch it compress as TradFi balance sheets enter crypto lending.
insights.quote: crypto capital markets are still more expensive than traditional capital markets on a riskadjusted basis in my opinion

insights.claim: Galaxy One's crypto portfolio line of credit lets users borrow cash against Bitcoin, or a combined Bitcoin/Ethereum/Solana portfolio, at a rate below 9% with no origination fees, monthly interest and full prepayment flexibility — which Prince claims is the best rate available in centralized crypto finance.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: A concrete benchmark for the current cost of crypto-collateralized borrowing; competitors pricing materially above 9% are losing the CeFi lending market.

insights.claim: Galaxy One borrowers continue to earn Solana staking rewards — roughly 6% — on assets posted as collateral, which Pompliano frames as an effective blended cost of capital near 3% against a sub-9% borrow rate.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: Staking-while-collateralized materially changes the economics of levered crypto positions and is a differentiator worth checking at every lender.
insights.quote: while you have your assets staked, uh if you're staking Salana and borrowing against it, you still earn the Salana staking rewards um even while they're posted as collateral

insights.claim: Galaxy One offers Solana staking at zero commission through the end of the year by piggybacking on Galaxy's existing institutional staking infrastructure, versus the 20-30% of staking rewards Prince says competing platforms charge.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: Staking commission is a 20-30% haircut most retail holders never price; vertical integration is being used to compete that fee toward zero.
insights.quote: we're actually offering staking with zero commissions currently through the end of the year. um compare that to, you know, 20 25 30% that you're paying in uh fees

insights.claim: Galaxy One will not offer prediction markets or superleveraged products, with Prince arguing such instruments are hard to fit into any long-term portfolio even though platforms can charge around 5% per event-contract trade.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: Names the take rate driving the prediction-market land grab and identifies a deliberate segmentation: volume-based trading platforms versus long-term balance-sheet platforms.
insights.quote: I don't think platforms like that are where investors are going to manage large percentages of their long-term capital

insights.claim: Pompliano counters that prediction-market and event-contract platforms are not even competing for long-term savings — they target trading assets, so a savings account and a trading account will naturally optimize for different things.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Suggests the two models can coexist rather than converge; wallet-share analysis should separate trading balances from nest-egg balances.

themes.theme: Where Prince Now Sees Crypto Opportunity

insights.claim: Prince's personal risk appetite for crypto decreased tremendously after the crypto war and he now finds more excitement in traditional brokerage accounts than in the crypto market — a striking reversal for a man who was blogging in 2015 telling readers to get Bitcoin and Ethereum exposure.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: A founder who built the largest crypto yield platform now routing to TradFi wrappers is a sentiment marker for where crypto-native talent and capital are migrating.
insights.quote: I'm not interested in having a tussle with regulators again.

insights.claim: For the average US consumer Prince's advice is now to buy whichever spot ETF brand you have the best affinity to among BlackRock, Fidelity and Bitwise and hold it in a brokerage account, rather than using a crypto platform.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: Reinforces that US retail crypto flows are structurally routing through ETF issuers, compressing the addressable market for consumer crypto platforms domestically.
insights.quote: buy buy whatever brand you have the best affinity to between BlackRock, Fidelity, Bitwise, and you know, a couple other ETF issuers and put it in your brokerage account

insights.claim: Prince locates the remaining high-value crypto opportunity outside the US — stablecoin adoption and tokenizing real-world assets including stocks to democratize access to US markets — while inside the US he sees it mainly as securities-infrastructure plumbing: faster settlement and on-chain transparency.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: A geographic bifurcation of the crypto thesis: consumer-facing upside is ex-US, US upside is B2B infrastructure sold into the existing securities stack.

insights.claim: Prince wants to unbundle the traditional registered investment advisor model, on the view that investors increasingly understand a 1% AUM fee is a major long-term portfolio drag but still want specific pieces of what RIAs do without paying for the whole bundle.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: Names the strategic wedge for the next generation of self-directed platforms and the fee pool — roughly 1% of AUM — that is under attack.
insights.quote: I like this concept of unbundling the traditional registered investment advisor model.

insights.claim: Pompliano reports finding an ordinary US financial advisor charging up to a 1.75% management fee, with volume discounts, and argues it is remarkable that such fees persist in 2026 for average solutions.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: The observed 1.75% top-of-book advisory fee sets the ceiling that low-cost unbundled competitors will undercut — check the ADV before assuming 1% is the market rate.
insights.quote: They charge up to a 1.75% management fee

insights.claim: Prince argues the standard 60/40 portfolio advisors default clients into is inappropriate for many investors, and that someone under 40 — arguably even under 50 or 60 — does not need a 40% bond allocation and can reasonably be 100% in equities or equity-like instruments.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: If platforms productize this, it shifts marginal retail allocation away from fixed income toward equities and equity-like assets across a large demographic cohort.
insights.quote: if you're under the age of 40, I don't think you need a 40% allocation to bonds

insights.claim: Pompliano cites TLT being down 50% over the last five years as the chart that undermines the case for bonds in young investors' portfolios, noting the standard pushback that it is 'not real bonds.'
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Long-duration Treasury drawdown is the empirical anchor for the anti-60/40 argument now being built into consumer products.
insights.quote: Down 50% in the last 5 years

insights.claim: Prince believes a conservative 10-30% leverage overlay on a young investor's portfolio is mathematically sound per academic research, explicitly distinguishing it from the 2x-5x leverage available on perpetual futures, and says Galaxy One has products coming in the next months to make that view accessible.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: Lifecycle-leverage as a mainstream retail product is a new category to watch — it expands margin-lending balances and changes retail drawdown behavior.
insights.quote: is it a bad thing to put a conservative amount of leverage on that portfolio? When I say conservative amount of leverage, I'm talking like in the 10 to 30% range

insights.claim: Prince plans to extend Galaxy One's portfolio line-of-credit model from crypto collateral to brokerage account assets and later to real estate and other lending, positioning the app as full asset-and-liability balance sheet management rather than a trading venue.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: Signals the roadmap: the competitive battleground is consumer liabilities, not just assets, and private-bank-style lending is being unbundled to self-directed investors.

insights.claim: Prince identifies mundane private-bank operational features — notably easy repeat wire sending for VC capital calls or contractor payments — as an underrated product wedge, noting many people still must visit a branch or manually retype wire instructions.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: Operational friction, not yield, may be the actual switching cost for high-net-worth self-directed clients — a cheap moat for whoever automates it first.

themes.theme: Agentic Finance and Galaxy's AI Data Center Business

insights.claim: Galaxy One is actively debating two architectures for AI agents in finance — exposing permissioned interfaces so users can point any external agent at the app, or building agent functionality natively — and is weighing ending up with both while working through compliance and security risks of third-party AI executing financial transactions.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: The external-agent-permissions vs native-agent choice is the coming fork for every fintech; liability for an unwanted third-party-agent action is the unresolved blocker.
insights.quote: That's certainly um could get risky if somebody has a third party AI that they give access to our system and then it does something that the user doesn't like.

insights.claim: Galaxy now has two large businesses — the crypto business spanning institutional financial services and the retail Galaxy One app, and an AI data center business with a greater-than-5-gigawatt power pipeline primarily at its Helios campus in Texas and now spanning multiple campuses.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: Galaxy's equity is no longer a pure crypto-beta instrument; the 5+ GW pipeline makes it partly an AI-power infrastructure play with a different set of comparables.
insights.quote: it's also now in the AI data center business with uh a larger than 5 gawatt power pipeline um in Texas

insights.claim: Prince expects interesting crossover applications over time between Galaxy's crypto financial services and its AI data center business, framing the firm's internal culture as incredibly AI-forward.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: Any announced crypto/AI-infrastructure crossover from Galaxy would be a re-rating catalyst; the thesis is currently exploratory rather than specified.

insights.claim: Galaxy has taken naming rights on Texas Tech's football stadium, now referred to as Galaxy Stadium in Lubbock, Texas — a consumer brand-building spend consistent with its retail push.
insights.speaker: Zac Prince
insights.so_what: Mass-market sponsorship spend signals Galaxy is funding a genuine retail customer-acquisition campaign, not just an institutional franchise.
